readerTitle: Why a free taste in the aisle sells more than a coupon
caseNote: 실제 기업 관찰 (Costco 등 창고형 매장의 시식) + 실제 연구 (Strohmetz 외 2002, 계산서와 함께 준 사탕과 팁) + 가상 적용 (차 전문점, 포장재 제조사)
insight: 작은 선물이 효과를 내는 이유는 값어치가 아니라, 먼저 아무 조건 없이 사람이 직접 건넸다는 데 있다. 같은 비용이라도 할인보다 선물이 더 강한 답례를 끌어낼 수 있다.
misconception: 고객은 가격만 따지므로, 줄 수 있는 돈이 있으면 할인으로 주는 게 가장 효과적이다. 선물은 비쌀수록 효과가 크다.

sources.text: Strohmetz, D. B., Rind, B., Fisher, R., & Lynn, M. (2002). Sweetening the till: The use of candy to increase restaurant tipping. Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 32(2), 300–309.
Cialdini, R. B. (1984). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion. (상호성 원칙과 무료 시식 사례)
Costco의 매장 내 시식 운영에 관한 언론 보도 (일반적 사실만 사용)

factChecks.note: Costco 등 창고형 매장이 매장 내 무료 시식으로 잘 알려져 있다는 일반적 사실만 썼습니다. 시식으로 인한 판매 증가율 같은 구체적 수치는 출처가 불분명해 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 시식 운영 방식(외부 업체 운영 여부 등)을 다시 확인하세요.
Strohmetz 외(2002) 연구: 사탕 1개는 팁이 약 3%, 2개는 약 14%, 1개를 준 뒤 돌아와 하나를 더 준 조건은 약 21~23% 증가로 보고된 것으로 알려져 있습니다. 정확한 수치를 원문에서 확인하기 전까지 카드에는 퍼센트 없이 크기 순서만 적었습니다.
B2B 선물 규정(구매 담당자의 선물 수령 제한)은 회사·국가마다 다르므로 특정 법률 조언 없이 일반론으로만 다뤘습니다.

cards.title: Why a free taste in the aisle sells more than a coupon
body: Walk through a warehouse store like Costco on a weekend and you'll find people in aprons handing out bites of cheese, dumplings and cookies.
A cube of cheese costs the store very little. Yet many shoppers who take one end up putting a box in their cart. Trying the food explains part of it. Something else explains the rest.

image.label: A shopper taking a free sample from a smiling staff member
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 창고형 매장 통로에서 앞치마를 두른 직원이 작은 종이컵에 담긴 시식을 쇼핑객에게 건네는 장면. 쇼핑객의 카트 옆 선반에 같은 상품 상자. 실제 매장 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your new tea isn't selling.
body: You run a small tea shop. A new blend sits on the shelf at $12 a tin, and few people try it. You have a small budget to push it this month.
Which approach would you bet on?

options.text: Put up a sign: 15% off the new blend
options.feedback: A discount lowers the barrier, but you give up margin on every tin, including tins people would have bought anyway. It also teaches customers to wait for the next deal.

options.text: Have staff pour a small fresh cup for each customer and chat about it
options.feedback: Customers taste the tea, and they receive something from a person, unasked. That small gift creates a pull to give something back.

options.text: Set out a self-serve tray of sample cups with a sign
options.feedback: Cheaper on staff time, and people still get to taste it. But a tray feels like a display, not a gift, so much of the pull is lost.

cards.title: A sample is also a small gift.
body: A free taste does two jobs. It lets customers try the product with no risk. And it puts them, very slightly, in your debt.
Many shoppers feel a little awkward taking food and walking away. A person smiled, handed them something and asked nothing in return. Buying a box quietly settles the account.
The gift is worth cents. The feeling it creates is worth far more.

cards.title: Reciprocity
body: **Reciprocity** is the strong human urge to return a favor, even one we never asked for.

It runs through almost every culture. People who receive something tend to give back, often more than they got. Psychologist Robert Cialdini listed it among the core principles of persuasion in his 1984 book *Influence*, using free samples as a classic example.

image.label: Two hands passing a small gift and a larger one coming back
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 손이 작은 선물 상자를 건네고, 오른쪽에서 더 큰 상자가 화살표를 따라 돌아오는 순환 구조. 위에 "Give first", 아래에 "Get back more" 라벨.

cards.title: Two mints and a tip.
body: In a 2002 study, researchers had restaurant servers bring a check with or without candy.
One piece of candy raised tips a little. Two pieces raised them more. Tips rose the most when the server left one candy, walked away, then came back with a second one "for you nice people."
The candy was the same. What changed was how personal and unexpected the gift felt.

image.label: Three restaurant checks with zero, one and two mints
image.brief: 계산서 접시 3개를 나란히. 왼쪽은 사탕 없음, 가운데는 사탕 1개, 오른쪽은 사탕 2개와 웃으며 돌아오는 직원의 손. 각 접시 위 팁 동전 더미가 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 점점 높아짐. 숫자는 넣지 않음.

cards.title: Not all gifts pull equally.
body: The value of the gift matters less than how it is given. Gifts pull hardest when they are:
list: **First:** given before you ask for anything
**Personal:** handed over by a person, not left on a tray
**Unexpected:** a surprise, not a standard perk
cards.callout: A $1 surprise from a person can beat a $5 discount on a sign.
cards.softwareNote: Software companies use reciprocity when they give away a genuinely useful free tool, template or guide before asking for a sign-up. It works best when the free thing solves a real problem on its own.

cards.title: A gift with strings is a bribe.
body: If the gift is clearly a trick, the pull flips. People who feel manipulated push back and remember who did it.
The urge to repay can also feel uncomfortable. Pressure customers too hard and they may avoid your aisle next time.

And gifts that repeat become expected. A free coffee every visit stops being a gift and becomes part of the price. In business-to-business sales, many buyers also have rules about accepting gifts at all.

cards.title: Now it's a packaging factory.
body: You make shipping boxes and protective packaging. You want to win a large food company as a customer. Its buyer has used the same supplier for years.
Which first move gives you the best chance?

options.text: Send the buyer's team a luxury gift basket before the holidays
options.feedback: It may break the buyer's gift rules and looks like an attempt to buy influence. You risk losing trust before the first meeting.

options.text: Offer a free check of where their shipments get damaged, with no strings attached
options.feedback: It's useful, personal and given first. Even if they don't switch right away, they now owe you a fair hearing, and you've learned their real problems.

options.text: Offer 5% off the first order if they sign this month
options.feedback: A clear incentive, but it's a deal, not a gift. It asks for a commitment before you've given anything, so it creates little pull to return the favor.

cards.title: Give first, give personally, and ask for nothing.
body: People want to repay what they receive. A small, useful, unexpected gift from a real person often moves customers more than a discount of the same cost.
**Try it today:** list one small thing you could give customers before they buy. Ask: is it useful, personal and free of strings?
